summary:
Roraima stands under Brazil's national framework rather than its own state statute. Same-sex marriage has been legal nationwide since the National Council of Justice Resolution of 14 May 2013, carried 14-1, joint adoption has been available since 2010 with full rights from 2015, and the Supreme Federal Court ruling of 1 March 2018 removed surgery, hormones or a diagnosis as conditions for changing a name and gender marker. No state-level deviation from those provisions is recorded for Roraima, and a visitor's status and documents are handled on the same footing as anyone else's at entry and in family matters.

On 13 June 2019 the Supreme Federal Court ruled in ADO 26 and MI 4733 that discrimination and violence motivated by sexual orientation or gender identity constitute a crime equivalent to racism under Law 7.716/1989, punishable by imprisonment of one to five years and fines. An OAB/SP guide for expatriates places these among the most progressive LGBTQ protections in Latin America on paper, while stating plainly that enforcement is uneven in practice.

Identity documents follow the national rules. There is no third-gender option on documents nationwide, though civil-registry entries recording a non-binary or unspecified gender have been possible since 2020 and a Superior Court of Justice ruling of 6 May 2025 permits rectification of a registry entry to a neutral gender as precedent. Gender-marker change proceeds by self-determination.

Arrest carries a specific placement regime. National Council of Justice Resolution 348 of 13 October 2020, amended by Resolution 366 of 20 January 2021, governs where LGBTI people who are arrested or imprisoned are housed. LGBTI status is recognised by self-declaration before a judge, including at a custody hearing, and the judge must consult the person on whether they prefer a female, male or LGBTI-specific unit and, within it, the general population or a specific wing or cell. LGBTI-specific spaces may not be used as disciplinary isolation and compulsory transfer as punishment is prohibited.

The protective text does not describe what people routinely encounter. OutRight International reports that Brazil retains one of the highest rates of violence against sexual and gender minorities in the world, particularly affecting trans people, and that its legal advances face repeal pressure in a conservative Congress. Outright's country overview records that LGBTIQ people still face significant violence and discrimination despite the constitutional and criminal provisions.

Where in the country a visitor is matters to daily exposure. Major cities including São Paulo, Rio de Janeiro, Brasília, Belo Horizonte, Curitiba and Florianópolis are described as broadly welcoming, with established legal infrastructure, while smaller cities and rural areas may present more social friction despite identical legal rights. Boa Vista and Roraima's other centres are not among the cities identified as having that infrastructure.
tangentialFactors:
Brazil's national legislature contains organised pressure against the existing framework. OutRight International records that the country's significant LGBTIQ legal advances face repeal pressure in a conservative Congress, so protections that a visitor relies on are contested politically even where they are settled in law.

Political representation of trans people has moved quickly. The first transgender federal legislators, Salabert and Hilton, were elected in 2022, and over 3,000 openly LGBTQ candidates ran in the 2024 municipal elections. In the October 2024 municipal elections close to 1,000 transgender candidates stood across every state of the country and received death threats and intimidation, while the number of trans officeholders tripled compared with the previous cycle.

The comparison class for a visitor arriving from elsewhere in the region is favourable on paper. An OAB/SP guide for expatriates places Brazil among the most progressive jurisdictions in Latin America for LGBTQ protections, covering same-sex marriage under CNJ Resolution 175/2013, joint adoption, name and gender-marker change without surgery, and the criminalisation of homophobia and transphobia as equivalent to racism.

Violence risk is documented independently of the legal text. A May 2024 investigation documented 'boa noite, Cinderela' drink-spiking robberies in which LGBTQIA+ people are targeted in São Paulo nightlife, in a city preparing for a Pride event that draws thousands of tourists. Courts have also applied the anti-discrimination provisions to commercial conduct: the 27th Private Chamber of the São Paulo Court of Justice upheld a moral-damage award against a nightclub that refused entry to a trans woman wearing women's clothing.

Protection machinery has widened. An analysis of case law from 2022 records lower courts pressing the Superior Court of Justice toward unanimously extending the remedies of the Maria da Penha Law and the Feminicide Law to trans women, bringing trans people within the country's violence-prevention statutes.
localsOnly:
Residents may change their legal gender marker by self-determination, without surgery, hormones or a diagnosis, under the Supreme Federal Court ruling of 1 March 2018. Civil registries have been able to record a non-binary or unspecified gender since 2020, and the Superior Court of Justice ruling of 6 May 2025 allows rectification of a registry entry to a neutral gender as precedent, although there is no third-gender option on identity documents nationally.

Trans voters may register under their lived name and identity even before their documents are updated. Same-sex couples hold the full range of marriage and adoption rights on the same terms as other couples.

Housing in detention is decided case by case. A person's declared preference is recorded, a later change of placement is possible, and transfers are prioritised where there is violence or a serious threat. The same national rules apply in Roraima's custodial facilities as elsewhere in the country.

Roraima's residents live under national court rulings and national administration on these questions. The inventory records no Roraima state statute on LGBTI matters and no state-level departure from the national framework.
outOfScopeNotes:
No Roraima-specific incident data appears in the source inventory. There is no sourced account of a hate-crime prosecution, an assault against a trans person, or a detention placement decision inside Roraima, so the risk picture for the state is inferred from the national pattern rather than documented locally.

The claim that Boa Vista lacks the established LGBTI legal infrastructure found in the named major cities rests on the expatriate guide's list of welcoming cities, which does not include it. Absence from that list is not evidence of hostility, and no source assesses conditions in Roraima's capital directly.

Whether the Superior Court of Justice's neutral-gender registry precedent of 6 May 2025 has been applied by civil registries in Roraima is unresolved in the inventory, as is whether the detention-placement guarantees of Resolutions 348 and 366 have been followed in the state's facilities. Neither is documented either way in the sources supplied.

OutRight International's reporting on repeal pressure in Congress gives no indication of which provisions are targeted or of any legislative progress, and the inventory carries no date for that specific finding. Roraima's own legislative output on sexual-orientation and gender-identity grounds is not sourced at all.
